title: Microstructural evolution of secondary carbides during spheroidized annealing and quenching and tempering in 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel
abstract: The microstructural changes in secondary carbides during spheroidized annealing (SA) and quenching and tempering (QT) processes in 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel has been comprehensively studied. Using scanning electron microscope, X-ray diffraction, inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry, and transmission electron microscopy, a substantial dissolution of submicron-sized M23C6 carbides after QT treatment was observed, leading to an increase in the mean carbides diameter. The highest solubility occurs at a 0.5 μm diameter, and carbide roundness improves during QT. Notably, the transformation of M7C3 carbides into M23C6 carbides was observed in QT samples through a multi-site in-situ nucleation mechanism. Additionally, it has been observed that Nb-rich MC carbides effectively restrict the growth of alloy carbides during heat treatment.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel is a new type of high-carbon martensitic stainless steel (HCMSS) known for its excellent strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, and wear resistance. This material is utilized in the production of premium knives and scissors due to its ability to maintain sharpness and durability [ 1–3 ].

In HCMSS, carbide formation is an inevitable secondary phase resulting from composition and process design, attracting attention not only for the benifits of enhanced mechanical properties but also the risks associated with segregation [ 4 ]. These carbides are classified into primary carbides and secondary carbides according to the precipitation sequence [ 5 ]. Primary carbides are generally large in size and irregular in shape, which may damage the whole properties of steel significantly [ 6 , 7 ]. Consequently, extensive research has been dedicated not only to optimizing alloy composition [ 8 ], but also refining control during subsequent process steps [ 9 , 10 ] and heat treatment procedures [ 11 ]. However, in recent years, attention has increasingly shifted toward secondary carbides, which are smaller in size and typically contribute to reinforcing the matrix of steel [ 12–14 ]. The microstructural characteristics of secondary carbides, including their volume fraction [ 15 ], type [ 16–20 ], size [ 21 ], morphology [ 22–24 ] and distribution [ 25 , 26 ], exert a critical influence on steel performance. In martensitic stainless steel, three predominant types of secondary carbides are recognized, each distinguish by its crystal structure: MC, M 7 C 3  and M 23 C 6  (‘M’ represents the alloy elements) [ 18–20 ]. Among these, MC carbides are formed by the preferential combination of strong carbide forming elements such as Nb and V with carbon [ 27 , 28 ], which will inhibit the formation of Cr-rich carbides [ 20 , 29 ]. Muchiri [ 30 ] and Hua [ 31 ] et al. reported that hardness of MC carbides were over 20 GPa, which will help to achieve dispersion strengthening easily. In contrast, M 7 C 3  carbides have greater mechanical properties include Pugh's ratio B/G [ 32 ], Poisson's ratio and hardness [ 33–37 ], and should be the superior secondary precipitations that improves the wear resistance of steel to M 23 C 6 . However, M 7 C 3  carbides are habitually precipitated in a morphology of coarse, network or films separated in grain boundary, which will significantly deteriorate the wear resistance [ 38 ] and fracture toughness [ 39 ] of steel. Consequently, fine and uniform M 23 C 6  carbides are more desired in HCMSS.

Recent research findings indicate that the strengthening effect of complex structure carbides surpasses that of individual carbides [ 40 ]. Consequently, there has been a growing focus on investigating the existence and transformation of complex carbides characterized by core-shell or bull ‘s-eye structure. Most studies on core-shell structure involving M 7 C 3 /M 23 C 6  destinate primary M 7 C 3  as the core, with a secondary M 23 C 6  shell forming at the junction of M 7 C 3  and matrix [ 41–44 ]. The prevailing discourse suggests that this transformation is likely governed by carbon diffusion [ 43 ] and the migration of chromium atoms [ 44 , 45 ]. Additionally, the crystal structure stability of different carbides significantly influences the transformation process of complex carbides. Notably, Wieczerzak et al. [ 41 ] have found that the orthorhombic M 7 C 3  carbides transform in-situ into the cubic M 23 C 6  carbides, characterized by a higher symmetry of crystal structure, within the Fe–25Cr-0.8C alloy at temperature ranging from 500 to 600 °C. However, there are also some studies have reported complex carbides with M 23 C 6  carbide cores and M 7 C 3  carbide shell under various steel compositions and dissimilar preparation processes [ 46 , 47 ].

Currently, research on carbide transition behavior primarily centers on materials such as Ni-based superalloys [ 40 , 48 ], high-chromium cast iron [ 42 , 49–51 ], HP-MA [ 43 , 47 ] and others [ 41 , 45 ], emphasizing the kind of primary carbides [ 44 ]. However, the study of secondary carbides transformation behavior in HCMSS with distinct compositions remains notably underexplored. Therefore, this paper quantitatively compares carbide characteristics in 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel under spheroidized annealing (SA) and quenching and tempering (QT) conditions. Additionally, we present evidence of multi-site in-situ transformation from M 7 C 3  carbides to M 23 C 6  carbides following QT, along with insights into controlling carbide size through the appropriate presence of Nb-rich MC carbides.

sections.heading: Material and methods
paragraphs:
The materials used in this study were commercial spheroidal annealed 60Cr16MoMA plate with a thicknesses of 5.5 mm. Chemical compositions of the investigated steel are shown in  Table 1 
                      . The SA specimens were subjected to austenitization at 1075 °C for 35 min, followed by oil quenching and tempering at 160 °C for 1 h.

Microstructural analysis was carried out using a ZEISS SIGMA 300 thermal field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). Metallographic samples sized 10 × 10 × 5 mm were polished and etched using a solution of 5 g FeCl 3  + 25 ml HCl +25 ml ethanol. Over ten randomly selected fields of view were examined for each sample. The volume fraction, size and roundness of carbides were quantitatively analyzed using image analysis software. Material thermodynamics and kinetics simulation software were employed to calculate the phase composition and precipitation sequence during equilibrium phase precipitation.

To facilitate accurate qualitative and quantitative analysis of carbides, the samples were machined into dimentions of 33 × 33 × 5 mm. Subsequently, they were dissolved in a solution consisting of 1 % lithium chloride and 10 % acetyl acetone solution, to achieve precipitation using an electrolytic extraction technique. The extracted precipitation was filtered using a microporous filter film, washing in a 10 g/L citric acid ethanol solution, thoroughly dried at 70 °C and collected. Phase constitutions were determined through X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis using a X'Pert Pro MPD instrument equipped with a Cu-K α  tube, with a step size of 0.0167° and a scanning speed of 5°/s −1 , operating at 40 kV and 150 mA. To quantify the precipitation, it was washed three times, initially with a 10 g/L citric acid ethanol solution, followed by a 10 g/L citric acid solution, and finally distilled water. The filter film and precipitation were then transferred to a Teflon beaker containing 10 ml HCl, 1 ml HNO 3  and 1 ml HF for sample dissolution, followed by diluted with water in a 100 ml Teflon volumetric flask at a constant volume. The content of each element was determined using an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometer (ICP-AES) [ 52 ].

For further characterization of the precipitation (morphology, crystal structure, etc), transmission electron microscope (TEM) experiments were performed using a JEM-2100F microscope operating at 200 kV. In this work, the TEM specimens contained extracted carbides powder and carbon extraction replicas. For the powder samples, an appropriate quantity of powder mixed with an ethanol solution, subjected to ultrasonic agitation for 15–30 min, and then the carbide solution was applied to an ultra-thin carbon film copper grid using a rubber head dropper and allowed to dry. The carbon extraction replicas samples were prepared by evaporating the carbon film from the specimens priviously etched in a solution of 5 g FeCl 3  + 25 ml HCl +25 ml ethanol, followed by immersion in a 7 g FeCl 3  + 25 ml HCl +25 ml ethanol to remove the carbon film, including the precipitates, from the specimens.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
Fig. 1 (a) and (c) 
                       are the typical SEM images of SA and QT samples, respectively, and  Fig. 1 (b) and (d)  depict the colored images highlighting the carbides in the two samples. Notably, the QT treatment results in a substaintial reduction in overall carbides counts, especially in the case of submicron sized carbides. The distribution of carbides becomes more uniform and dispersed, with an observable improvement in carbide roundness.

Detailed quantitative statistical results are presented in  Table 2 
                      . After QT treatment, the volume fraction of carbides decreased from 9.9 vol % to 2.6 vol %, accompanied by a reduction in the maximum carbide diameter. However, both the average and minimum diameter of carbides were larger in the SA state.

Fig. 2 
                       (a) displays the distribution of the average carbide diameters collected from the same area in both SA and QT samples. After QT treatment, the observed carbide count decreased from 3842 to 878. In the SA sample, carbide sizes ranged from 0.3 to 3 μm, whereas in the QT sample, the range was slightly narrower, spanning from 0.3 to 2.6 μm. This indicates that some dissolution occurred among the larger carbides. The d mean , as shown in  Table 2  and is greater than their peak diameter in both the SA sample (0.5 μm) and QT sample (0.6 μm), resulting in a positively skewed size distribution in both samples. Moreover, the most significant reduction of 19 % is observed in carbides with a diameter of 0.5 μm after QT treatment.

Fig. 2  (b) shows the average size box-plot for both samples. The median value of SA and QT samples were 0.5 and 0.7 μm, respectively, indicating that a substantial number of carbides in the SA sample were smaller than those in the QT sample. The interquartile range of SA and QT samples was 0.32 and 0.55, respectively, implying that carbides in SA samples exhibited a better degree of aggregation among smaller sized. Moreover, compared to QT samples, carbides in SA samples have more outliers and a wider size range. Based on this analysis, a significant portion of carbides, especially those in the submicron range, dissolved into the matrix during the QT process, leading to the unexpected increase in the average carbide diameter in the QT sample.

The Roundness value increases with an increase in circularity and approaches 1 for a perfect circle [ 57 ].  Fig. 2  (b) shows the column diagram and Gaussian fitting curve of carbide roundness in SA and QT samples. In the SA sample, the highest frequency of roundness is at 0.80, while in the QT sample, it is at 0.90. The d X  in  Fig. 3 
                       provide an intuitive indicator of the roundness distribution of the analyzed carbides. The d 0.5  (d 0.9 ) indicates that 50 % (90 %) of the carbides are smaller than this value [ 58 ], which shown corresponding to the vertical dashed lines. In SA sample, d 0.5  and d 0.9  are 0.72 and 0.87, respectively. After QT treatment, these values increase to 0.80 (d 0.5 ) and 0.90 (d 0.9 ), respectively. Thus, the QT treatment significantly improves the roundness of the carbides.

The results discussed above revealed the dissolution of numerous small-sized carbides during the QT process. However, identifying the specific types of dissolved carbides by SEM images is challenging. The equilibrium solidification phase diagram of steel was derived through the thermodynamic software, as depicted in  Fig. 4 
                       (a). In 60Cr16MoMA steel, three carbides types are present: MC, M 23 C 6  and M 7 C 3 . Among them, MC carbides precipitated firstly at 1220 °C, with a rapid increase in content between 1220 °C and 1000 °C. M 7 C 3  carbides precipitated at 1190 °C, peaking at 0.01 vol % when the temperature dropping to 1152 °C. Moreover, this type of carbides rapidly decreased and vanished after cooling within 10 °C. However, M 23 C 6  carbides precipitated at 1150 °C, with its content surging as M 7 C 3  carbides content dropped. The transition from M 7 C 3  carbides to M 23 C 6  carbides is a recurring phenomenon in HCMSS [ 18 , 44 , 59 , 60 ]. The equilibrium phase diagram confirmed this transition in the experimental steel, notably between 1140 °C and 1155 °C. In addition, the observed carbides at room temperature comprised primarily M 23 C 6 , along with trace MC.

To obtain the crystal structure and morphology of carbides in the experimental steel, electrolytic extracted carbides were observed through XRD and TEM. As revealed in  Fig. 4  (b), MC carbides peaks alongside M 23 C 6  carbides in both SA and QT samples. This finding supports the predicted phase diagram.

Fig. 5 
                       shows the TEM images, selection electron diffraction (SAED) images, and energy disperse spectrometer (EDS) images of carbides in SA sample. The results indicate larger Cr and Fe-rich carbides correspond to M 23 C 6 , while smaller V and Nb-rich carbides are identified as MC carbides in the SA sample, both possessing a FCC crystal structure [ 28 , 61 ]. Furthermore, the presence of M 7 C 3  carbides connected with other carbides was observed in the SA sample, as described below.

Fig. 6 
                       diaplays high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) patterns, implying different types of carbides within the QT sample. In comparison to the SA sample, not only FCC-structured MC ( Fig. 6  (a)) and M 23 C 6  ( Fig. 6  (b)), but also orthogonal M 7 C 3  carbides ( Fig. 6  (c)) existed independently in the QT sample. Furthermore, the incomplete transformation of the M 7 C 3 /M 23 C 6  carbides were also observed in the QT samples.

Fig. 7 
                       (a) shows the HRTEM image of M 7 C 3 /M 23 C 6  complex structure carbides observed in the QT sample, and  Fig. 7  (b) displays the FFT analysis for selected carbides (indicated by the red box) in  Fig. 7  (a). The results reveal two distinct carbides types, M 23 C 6  and M 7 C 3  carbides. The crystal orientation relationship exists between the two carbides was identified as [101] M 7 C 3 //[001] M 23 C 6 . This alignment implies in-situ transformation within this carbide.

Remarkably, spheroidal carbides exhibiting multiple dark substructures were also found within the QT sample, as shown in  Fig. 8 
                       (a). The carbides corresponding to the red box in  Fig. 8  (a) were selected for HRTEM observation and analysis, as depicted in  Fig. 8  (b). The FFT pattern corresponding to the entire HRTEM ( Fig. 8  (b)) reveals diffraction rings of M 7 C 3  carbides in  Fig. 8  (c). However, local FFT ( Fig. 8  (d)) analysis of the darker region marked through red frame in the carbide HRTEM ( Fig. 8  (b)) reveals a different pattern corresponding to M 23 C 6  carbides. This signifies incomplete transformation of M 7 C 3 /M 23 C 6  complex structure carbides within the QT sample, where dark M 23 C 6  is in-situ transformed inside M 7 C 3  through multi-point nucleation.

Zhang [ 44 ] et al. conducted varing heat treatments on electroslag remelting samples of HCMSS, inducing an in-situ transformation from eutectic M 7 C 3  carbides to M 23 C 6  carbides. This transformation led to the formation of an M 23 C 6  shell at the boundary between M 7 C 3  and matrix, with the M 7 C 3  carbides serving as the core. In this study, the generation of M 23 C 6  carbides occurs through multi-point nucleation within the M 7 C 3  carbides via an in-situ transition mechanism.

In addition, a small quantity of MC carbides accompanies the major M 23 C 6  carbides, within the extracted samples. The elemental composition of extracted carbides determined using ICP-AES is summarized in  Table 3 
                      . The results yield specific composition for the carbides. For instance, (Cr 0·66 Fe 0·31 Mo 0·02 V 0.01 ) 23 C 6 , (Nb 0·39 V 0·54 Mo 0.07 )C in SA sample and (Cr 0·59 Fe 0·39 Mo 0·01 V 0.01 ) 23 C 6 , (Nb 0.87 V trace Mo 0.13 )C in QT sample. After the QT process, the content of Fe within M 23 C 6  carbides rises, while other alloying elements decreases. This is due to the dissolution of M 23 C 6  carbides during austenitizing, causing alloying elements and carbon to dissolve into the matrix [ 62 ]. In this process, two concentration gradients are formed between the undissolved carbides and the matrix. One is the alloying elements with high concentration in the undissolved carbides diffuse into the matrix, and the other is that the Fe element with high concentration in the matrix diffuses into the undissolved carbides [ 63 ]. Furthermore, a notable increase in Nb content, a significantly decline in V, and a slight elevation in Mo content are observed in MC carbides after the QT treatment. Nb's superior carbide-forming propensity compared to V, leads to heighten NbC precipitation and elevated melting temperature [ 64 ]. And it has been proved that NbC owns the best stability and lowest free energy compared to Cr 23 C 6 , Mo 2 C, Cr 7 C 3  and VC [ 18 ]. This causes NbC to remain and VC to dissolve under 1075 °C austenizing temperature in this study.

Fig. 9 
                       reveals fibrous carbides in addition to the globular carbide clusters observed in SA samples. In  Fig. 9  (a), certain fibrous carbides connect with spherical particles, while  Fig. 9  (b) presents independent fibrous carbides in distinct regions.

Fig. 10 
                       (a) shows the image of independently existed fibrous carbides, forming intricate interconnected structures. From this, two connection structures were selected for SAED analysis. The upper segment of the red box corresponds to orthogonal M 7 C 3  carbides ( Fig. 10  (b)), while the lower part presents hexagonal M 7 C 3  ( Fig. 10  (c)). The carbides encircled by the yellow box consists of the upper M 23 C 6  carbides ( Fig. 10  (d)) and the lower hexagonal M 7 C 3  carbides ( Fig. 10  (e)) connected. These results indicate that the fibrous carbides in the SA sample predominantly consist of M 7 C 3  carbides and M 23 C 6  carbides.

Fig. 11 
                       shows EDS analysis of selected independently existing fibrous carbides. STEM images revealed numerous white bright areas at the joints in  Fig. 11  (a), which corresponds to the yellow highlighted area in the red framed enlarged image. Further magnified examination in the EDS reveals that these white bright regions consist of Nb-rich MC carbides.  Fig. 11  (b) is the line scan analysis of the white bright carbides located at the carbides connection. Evident fluctuations in Nb content within the white bright area, definitively establish it as Nb-rich MC carbides.

In contrast, no fibrous carbides were observed in the QT sample. However, small MC carbides were found attached to large M 23 C 6  carbides in both QT and SA carbon film replicas, as shown in  Fig. 12 
                      . While most of the alloy carbides dissolve or transform after QT process, the small Nb-rich MC carbide particles remain unaffected during austenitization. These MC carbides retain their original locations, thus constraining the growth of other undissolved Cr-rich carbides around them.

Based on the findings of this study, the evolution of secondary carbides in 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel after QT is schematically illustrated in  Fig. 13 
                      . After QT treatment, the submicro-sized M 23 C 6  carbides, indicated by red dots, dissolved into the matrix, resulting in an increase in the average carbide diameter. Concurrently, the pointed regions of the larger, green, near-spherical carbides preferentially dissolved, leading to a significant improvement in their roundness. The QT sample also exhibited the presence of M 23 C 6 /M 7 C 3  complex carbides, wherein M 23 C 6  carbides, represented by pink pattern were observed nucleating at multiple points within M 7 C 3  carbides, gradually absorbing the M 7 C 3  carbides and growing in size. Furthermore, fibrous carbides were observed in the SA sample, often accompanied by the presence of orange-shaded Nb-rich MC carbides at nearly all junctions in this shape of carbide. The Nb-rich carbides exhibit remarkable resistance to dissolution during the austenitizing process, consequently impeding the growth of the surrounding Cr-rich carbides.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In conclusion, this study provides insights into secondary carbides evolution in 60Cr16MoMA martensitic stainless steel following quenching and tempering (QT): 
                         
                            (1) 
                            A significant reduction in carbide volume fraction from 9.9 vol % to 2.6 vol % after QT process, indicating substantial submicron-sized M 23 C 6  carbides dissolution during austenitization at 1075 °C and resulting in increased average carbide diameter. Most notably, 19 % dissolution occurred in 0.5 μm diameter carbides, alongside improved carbide roundness after QT. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Observation of M 7 C 3  to M 23 C 6  transformation in QT samples, revealing a multi-site, in-situ nucleation mechanism and shedding light on heat treatment-induced dynamic processes. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            Remarkable resistance of NbC in the SA sample to dissolution during QT, effectively impeding alloy carbide growth.
